title: The Light on Gull Rock
tagline: Someone is signalling from the empty lighthouse. Will you go and find out who?
blurb: You are on holiday in the seaside village of Gull Cove. The old lighthouse has been empty for years. So who switched on the light?

scene.alt: A lighthouse on a rock at night, its beam sweeping over the sea.

cast.label: The grown-up on holiday with you (Mum, Gran, Uncle Pete…)

chapters.title: The Empty Lighthouse

scene.alt: Gull Cove at sunset, with the old white lighthouse on its rock.

blocks: The car turned the last bend, and there was the sea.
{hero} pressed {hero.his} forehead to the window. Gulls hung in the air above the road. Beyond the rooftops of Gull Cove, a tall white tower stood alone on a rock at the end of the bay.
“That’s the old lighthouse,” said {grownup}.
“Does anyone live in it?” asked {friend}.
“Not for years. The rocks round it are dangerous, so nobody goes near.”
{pet} [[pet:dog=barked at the window|cat=put one paw flat against the glass]] as if {pet.he} {pet.has} an opinion about that.
Periwinkle Cottage sat at the top of a lane so narrow that the hedges scraped both sides of the car. It had a blue door, a crooked chimney and a garden gate that squeaked.
“Supper first,” said {grownup}. “Exploring tomorrow.”
Supper was fish and chips on the harbour wall, with a gull watching every single chip. The sun sank into the water. One by one, lights came on in the windows of the village.
By bedtime, the cottage creaked in every corner. {hero} and {friend} shared the room under the sloping roof, and {pet} curled up on the end of {hero.his} bed.
“Do you think anyone will ever live in the lighthouse again?” whispered {friend}.
“Maybe,” said {hero}. “If somebody fixed the light.”
{friend} did not answer. {friend.He} {friend.is} already breathing slowly.
Some time later, something woke {hero}. It was {pet}, standing on the bed with {pet.his} ears pricked and {pet.his} eyes fixed on the window.
{hero} crept across the cold floorboards and pulled back the curtain.

scene.alt: At night, the empty lighthouse glowing, its beam sweeping across black water.

blocks: Out on Gull Rock, the empty lighthouse was glowing. A beam of light swept slowly across the black water, once, twice. Then it stopped.
“{friend},” hissed {hero}. “Wake up. Now.”
{friend} was at the window in seconds. “That lighthouse is empty,” {friend.he} whispered.
“I know.”
The light began to blink. Three short flashes. A pause. Three long flashes. A pause. Three short flashes again.
“I’ve seen that in a book,” said {friend}. {friend.His} voice had gone very small. “It means someone needs help.”
Out in the dark, on a rock where nobody had lived for years, somebody was asking for help.

chapters.title: Three Short, Three Long

scene.alt: Periwinkle Cottage at night, one window still glowing.

blocks: “We have to tell {grownup},” said {friend}.
“And say what? That the empty lighthouse is winking at us?” {hero} looked back at the window. The light was still blinking. Three short. Three long. Three short.
{pet} jumped off the bed and trotted to the bedroom door. {pet.He} looked back at them. Waiting.

options.label: Sneak out and follow the signal right now
blocks: {hero} grabbed a torch and a coat. “Quietly,” {hero.he} whispered. Down the stairs they went, past {grownup}’s door, and out through the squeaky gate, which squeaked only once.

scene.alt: A dark path through the trees towards the glowing lighthouse.

options.label: Wake {grownup} and tell them everything
blocks: {hero} knocked softly on {grownup}’s door. It took a long time to explain. {grownup} did not laugh. {grownup.He} {grownup.was} out of bed and reaching for a phone before {hero} had finished talking.

scene.alt: Every window of the cottage now lit up.

options.label: Write down every flash, then work out a plan
blocks: {friend} found a notebook. {hero} found a pencil. Together they wrote down every flash, and the time of each one, until the pattern was perfectly clear. It never changed. Someone out there was very, very patient.

scene.alt: The first light of morning over Gull Cove.

blocks: Whatever happened next, one thing was certain. The lighthouse was not empty any more.

chapters.title: The Answer on the Rock

scene.alt: A bright, windy morning at Gull Rock.

blocks: Morning on Gull Rock was loud with wind.
{hero}’s socks were still wet from the night before, and the torch had a crack across its glass.
{grownup} had already phoned the harbour, and a small boat was putting out from the cove.
{friend} held the notebook open. Every flash of the night was written in it, with the time beside each one.
The tide was rising fast around the rocks, and a man was waving both arms from the lighthouse steps.
“Over here!” he shouted. “Please, over here!”

endings.title: The Brave Way

scene.alt: A small boat heading home from the lighthouse in bright sunshine.

blocks: {hero} did not wait for the boat. {hero.He} waded out along the sandbar with a rope round {hero.his} waist, the water cold and rising, and held out a hand.
The man was Old Tom, the fisherman. His engine had died in the night, and the lighthouse switch was the only thing he could find that still worked.
“Three short, three long, three short,” he said, laughing and shaking. “And somebody actually saw it.”
{pet} [[pet:dog=barked|cat=purred]] all the way home.

endings.title: The Kind Way

scene.alt: A boat full of people coming back from the lighthouse.

blocks: It was {grownup} who spotted the fisherman first, and it was {hero} who thought of the blanket and the flask of tea.
The man was Old Tom. His engine had died in the night, and the lighthouse switch was the only thing he could find that still worked.
“Most people would have gone back to sleep,” he said. “You woke the right person.”
That evening, the whole village came to Periwinkle Cottage with cake.

endings.title: The Clever Way

scene.alt: A boat reaching the lighthouse at dawn.

blocks: {friend} read out the notebook to the harbour master, line by line. The flashes had never changed, and neither had the time between them. “That is a person,” the harbour master said slowly. “Not a fault in the wiring.”
The man was Old Tom. His engine had died in the night, and the lighthouse switch was the only thing he could find that still worked.
“Every single flash, written down,” he said, shaking his head. “I’ve known coastguards who were less careful.”
